questions.q: Legally, what is a mortgage?
choices: The loan itself, as a contract
An interest in land given as security
A lease of the land to the lender
A guarantee from the government
questions.explain: A mortgage is an interest in land granted as security for a debt, plus evidence of that debt. It isn't the loan itself.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · What a mortgage is, legally

questions.q: Where did the equity of redemption come from?
choices: The Land Title Act, passed in 1990
The courts of equity, for fairness
The federal Interest Act of Canada
A 2014 Supreme Court of Canada ruling
questions.explain: Equity courts gave borrowers a right to redeem after the due date because forfeiting land for one late day was unfair.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Where the equity of redemption came from

questions.q: A home is worth $600,000 with a $150,000 mortgage. What is the owner's equity (in the everyday sense)?
questions.explain: Everyday equity is value minus debt: $600,000 − $150,000. Don't confuse it with the equity of redemption, which is a right.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Where the equity of redemption came from

questions.q: Against whom is an unregistered (equitable) mortgage enforceable?
choices: Against everyone, just like a legal one
Against the borrower, not third parties
Against third parties, but not the borrower
Against no one until it is registered
questions.explain: Equitable mortgages bind the borrower but not third parties. Registration is what gives effect against the world.

questions.q: What is needed for a deposit of the duplicate certificate of title to create an equitable mortgage?
choices: Registration at the land title office first
Delivery plus an intention to create security
A caveat filed in the lender's favour at once
A court order confirming the deposit was made
questions.explain: There must be actual delivery and an intent to create a mortgage; otherwise it may just be safekeeping (Mesa Estates).

questions.q: A loan is papered as an outright transfer of the land to the lender. How will a court treat it?
choices: As a valid sale; the borrower loses all
As a mortgage, restoring redemption
As void, with no security at all
As a lease to the lender
questions.explain: Courts look at substance. If the real purpose was security for a loan, it's a mortgage with an equity of redemption.

questions.q: Which mortgage term is a void "clog" on the equity of redemption?
choices: A restriction on prepaying the loan early
A lender's option to buy, granted with the loan
A clause that prohibits any assumption of the loan
A due on sale clause in the standard terms
questions.explain: An option to purchase given to the lender as part of the loan would stop redemption. Prepayment and assumption limits are not clogs.

questions.q: What did Bhasin v. Hrynew (SCC 2014) establish?
choices: Lenders can't foreclose without mediation
A duty of honest contract performance
A cap on mortgage interest rates
Oral promises always bind lenders
questions.explain: It recognized good faith as an organizing principle, including a duty to perform contracts honestly.

questions.q: If a lender's filed standard terms aren't given to and acknowledged by the borrower, which terms apply?
choices: None; the mortgage is void
The prescribed standard terms
The lender's filed terms anyway
Whatever the borrower chooses
questions.explain: The mortgage takes effect as if the Land Title Act's prescribed standard terms were used.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Express terms: the Form B mortgage

questions.q: Who decides whether to accelerate a mortgage after default?
choices: The borrower, by missing payments
The lender, at its option
The court, automatically
The land title registrar
questions.explain: Acceleration is at the lender's option. A lender wouldn't want a high-rate loan forced to end.

questions.q: How often can a court grant relief against acceleration for the same party and covenant?
choices: Never
Once
Twice
As often as needed
questions.explain: Law and Equity Act s.25 allows relief; s.28 limits it to once for the same party and covenant.

questions.q: What does an omnibus clause let a lender do?
choices: Accelerate the loan on any default at all
Pay unpaid taxes and add them to the loan
Refuse every further advance without notice
Vote on the owner's behalf at every meeting
questions.explain: If the borrower fails to pay something like taxes or strata fees, the lender can pay it and add it to the mortgage.

questions.q: A mortgage has no due on sale clause. What follows?
choices: The mortgage is void on any sale
The mortgage is assumable
The buyer must refinance
The seller must prepay it
questions.explain: Without a due on sale (or similar) clause, a buyer can assume the mortgage.

questions.q: How does a covenantor differ from a guarantor?
choices: A covenantor is only secondarily liable, like a guarantor
A covenantor is primarily liable, like the borrower
A covenantor can never be sued on the covenant
A covenantor pays only the interest, never principal
questions.explain: A covenantor is a primary debtor; a guarantor is liable only after the lender exhausts remedies against the borrower.

questions.q: What does an interim blanket mortgage on a development typically include?
choices: A ban on selling any of the lots
Partial discharges as units are sold
A vendor take-back on every unit
A fixed 25-year term
questions.explain: The lender releases each lot or strata unit as it's sold, keeping security over the rest.

questions.q: In a vendor take-back mortgage, who is registered as owner after completion?
choices: The seller, until the mortgage is fully paid
The buyer, with the seller's mortgage on title
The seller's own lender, as security trustee
The buyer and seller jointly, as co-owners
questions.explain: Title passes to the buyer; the seller's mortgage is registered against it. (In an agreement for sale, the seller stays on title.)

questions.q: What is bridge financing?
choices: A long-term loan used to fund infrastructure
Short-term interim financing at a higher rate
A second mortgage registered on a vacation home
A long-term loan insured by CMHC at a low rate
questions.explain: A short-term loan while long-term financing is arranged, e.g. buying before the old home sells.

questions.q: A loan document requires interest but states no rate. What rate applies under s.3?
choices: 5% a year
The prime rate
The criminal rate
questions.explain: Section 3 sets 5% per annum where no rate is stated.

questions.q: A blended-payment mortgage omits the required yearly or half-yearly rate statement. What's the result?
choices: The lender may charge prime instead
No interest can be charged
Interest is reduced to 5%
The mortgage is void entirely
questions.explain: Under s.6, if the required statement is missing, no interest is chargeable.

questions.q: A mortgage cuts the rate by 2% unless the borrower defaults. What did Krayzel (SCC 2016) say about that?
choices: It's fine; it simply rewards good borrowers
It breaches s.8: a higher rate on default
It's a clog on the equity of redemption
It's a criminal rate of interest under the Code
questions.explain: Losing a discount on default means paying more on arrears than on other principal, which s.8 forbids.

questions.q: How is a lender's bonus treated under the Interest Act and the Criminal Code?
choices: Interest under both of the two statutes
Principal (Interest Act) but interest (Code)
Interest (Interest Act) but principal (Code)
Ignored entirely by both of the statutes
questions.explain: Case law treats a bonus as principal for s.6 of the Interest Act, but the Criminal Code's broad definition counts it as interest.

questions.q: Which borrower can use the Interest Act s.10 prepayment right?
choices: A corporation after 5 years
An individual after 5 years
A partnership after 3 years
Any borrower after 1 year
questions.explain: Only individuals. Corporations never could; partnerships, ULCs and business trusts lost it for mortgages made from 2012.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Section 10: the five-year prepayment right

questions.q: An individual's mortgage is renewed and re-dated to the renewal date for a new 5-year term. When can they use s.10?
choices: Right away, as 5 years have passed
Not during the renewal term
After 3 months' notice
Only with the lender's consent
questions.explain: Re-dating restarts the clock, and a 5-year renewal isn't longer than 5 years, so s.10 doesn't help.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Section 10: the five-year prepayment right

questions.q: What must the borrower pay to prepay under s.10?
choices: The full interest to the end of the term
Everything owing plus 3 months' interest
An interest rate differential
Six months' interest
questions.explain: All principal and interest owing plus three months' interest. Then no further interest can be charged.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Section 10: the five-year prepayment right

questions.q: When does a lender lose its right to a prepayment penalty?
choices: When market rates rise above the contract rate
Once it accelerates and demands payment
After the first 3 years of the term pass
Whenever the borrower decides to sell
questions.explain: Once the balance is accelerated and demanded (e.g. foreclosure starts), the penalty is lost.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Section 10: the five-year prepayment right

questions.q: Since January 1, 2025, what is the criminal rate of interest?
choices: An effective rate over 60%
An APR over 35%
An APR over 48%
Any rate over prime + 10%
questions.explain: An annual percentage rate over 35%. Before 2025 it was an effective rate over 60%.

questions.q: A commercial loan of $750,000 to a corporation. Is it subject to a criminal rate?
choices: Yes, an APR over 35%
No criminal rate applies
Yes, an APR over 48%
Yes, an effective rate over 60%
questions.explain: Business loans to non-individuals over $500,000 are exempt. From $10,000 to $500,000 the cap is 48% APR.

questions.q: What happened in R. v. Frebold?
choices: A lender was fined for charging a high rate
A licensee was jailed for mortgage fraud
A buyer lost a bid at a foreclosure sale
A strata lien took priority over a mortgage
questions.explain: A licensee with a power of attorney diverted $672,000 of mortgage proceeds and altered documents: 30 months in prison.

questions.q: Under the Canmerica v. Yu test, what must a borrower first show to prove an unconscionable loan?
choices: That the rate charged exceeded 35% a year
Unequal bargaining power and unfairness
That they had no lawyer when they signed
That the lender was not licensed in BC
questions.explain: Inequality of bargaining power plus substantial unfairness; then the lender must prove the deal was fair.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act (BPCPA)

questions.q: How long before a consumer borrower is bound must the BPCPA disclosure statement be given?
choices: 1 day
2 days
7 days
21 days
questions.explain: Two days before the borrower incurs the obligation, unless waived. Renewal statements: 21 days before the term ends.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act (BPCPA)

questions.q: Which would make someone a mortgage broker under BC's Mortgage Brokers Act?
choices: Making 3 private mortgage loans a year
Earning $1,000+ a year arranging mortgages
Owning a mortgaged rental property
Referring one friend to a bank
questions.explain: Triggers include $1,000+ a year in fees arranging mortgages or making 10+ mortgage loans a year.

questions.q: When can a secured lender become liable to remediate a contaminated site?
choices: Whenever it lends money on a contaminated site
If it causes contamination or becomes owner
Only if the borrower goes bankrupt first
Never; BC law fully protects secured lenders
questions.explain: It's protected for financial involvement, but liable if it causes contamination through control or becomes registered owner (e.g. order absolute).

questions.q: Does a lender need the borrower's consent to assign a mortgage?
choices: Yes, always, and the consent must be in writing
No, but the borrower must get notice
Yes, plus a court order approving the transfer
Only for residential mortgages, not commercial
questions.explain: No consent is needed. Written notice to the borrower makes payments due to the assignee.

questions.q: A borrower pays the original lender $2,000 after receiving notice of assignment. What's the effect?
choices: The payment reduces the debt to the assignee
It doesn't reduce what's owed to the assignee
The assignment is cancelled
The assignee must refund the borrower
questions.explain: Notice freezes the accounts. Payments to the old lender after notice don't count against the assignee.

questions.q: After a buyer assumes the seller's mortgage, is the seller still liable?
choices: No, liability ends automatically
Yes, unless released or novated
Only if the buyer is a company
Only for the first year
questions.explain: The original borrower stays liable on the personal covenant unless released (PLA) or there's a novation.

questions.q: Can a lender sue a buyer who assumed the mortgage directly?
choices: No, because of privity of contract
Yes, the Property Law Act allows it
Only if the buyer signed a guarantee
Only for residential loans
questions.explain: The Property Law Act overrides privity and lets any lender sue an assuming buyer directly.

questions.q: To release the seller, within what time must the request for the lender's written approval of the buyer be made?
choices: 30 days of the transfer
3 months of the transfer
6 months of the transfer
1 year of the transfer
questions.explain: Within 3 months of the transfer. The lender can't unreasonably refuse for a residential-purpose loan.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Getting the seller released (Property Law Act)

questions.q: Which loan does NOT qualify for the Property Law Act release from continuing liability?
choices: A loan to buy the home
A business loan secured on the home
A loan to renovate the home
A refinance of a home purchase loan
questions.explain: Only residential-purpose loans qualify: buying or improving the residence, household spending, or refinancing those.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Getting the seller released (Property Law Act)

questions.q: The term of an assumed residential mortgage expires. When is the original borrower released if the lender does nothing?
choices: Immediately, as soon as the term expires
If no demand within 3 months of expiry
After 1 year without any demand being made
Never, without the lender's written approval
questions.explain: If the lender doesn't demand payment within 3 months after maturity, the original borrower's liability ends.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Getting the seller released (Property Law Act)

questions.q: Which is NOT required for a novation of a mortgage?
choices: The new borrower assumes complete liability
A court order approving the substitution
The lender accepts the new borrower as principal debtor
The new contract fully replaces the old one
questions.explain: No court order is needed. The three requirements are complete liability, acceptance as principal debtor, and full substitution.

questions.q: Lender B lends first but registers second; Lender C lends later but registers first. Who has first priority?
choices: Lender B, who lent first
Lender C, who registered first
They share first priority equally
Whoever lent the larger amount
questions.explain: In BC, priority follows the order of registration, not the date of the loan.

questions.q: How can a later-registered mortgage rank ahead of an earlier one?
choices: By charging a higher interest rate than the first
Through a registered priority agreement
By being the larger of the two loans
By being insured by CMHC or another insurer
questions.explain: Charge holders can rearrange priority with registered priority (postponement) agreements, or a mortgage can say it's subject to another.

questions.q: A third mortgagee forecloses to order absolute. What does it take?
choices: Title free and clear of all the mortgages
Title subject to the 1st and 2nd mortgages
Only the first mortgage's ranking position
Nothing; it must sell through the court instead
questions.explain: Redeem up, foreclose down: it forecloses only the borrower, so it owns subject to the senior mortgages.

questions.q: Which lets a first lender keep priority for a later construction advance over a registered second mortgage?
choices: Oral notice given by the second lender
A priority agreement with the second lender
Charging a higher interest rate on the advance
Making the advance within 30 days of registration
questions.explain: Priority is kept with no written notice, a contractual obligation to advance, or (most commonly) a priority agreement.

questions.q: Which claim beats a registered mortgage without being registered at all?
choices: A second mortgage registered later
Unpaid municipal property taxes
A builders lien that has been filed
A strata lien for unpaid strata fees
questions.explain: Property tax liens rank ahead of everything except the Crown and need no registration.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Statutory priorities: claims that can jump ahead of a registered mortgage

questions.q: After a municipal tax sale, how long does the owner or mortgagee have to redeem?
choices: 30 days
1 year
2 years
3 years
questions.explain: One year from the sale. Tax sales happen after 3 years of arrears (2 years for rural properties).
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Statutory priorities: claims that can jump ahead of a registered mortgage

questions.q: How does a filed builders lien rank against a registered mortgage?
choices: Behind the whole mortgage, in all cases
Ahead of advances made after filing
Ahead of the entire mortgage, always
Equal with the mortgage, sharing pro rata
questions.explain: The lien has priority over mortgage advances made after the date it's filed.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Statutory priorities: claims that can jump ahead of a registered mortgage

questions.q: Why are CRA deemed trust claims a special risk for lenders?
choices: They're always for amounts under $1,000
There's no registry to search for them
They rank behind every registered mortgage
They expire automatically after 30 days
questions.explain: Unremitted source deductions and GST can be claimed years later, and there's no registry to check.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Statutory priorities: claims that can jump ahead of a registered mortgage

questions.q: A business borrower is insolvent. How long must the lender wait after a BIA s.244 notice before enforcing?
choices: 5 days
10 days
15 business days
30 days
questions.explain: Ten days. For farmers, the Farm Debt Mediation Act requires 15 business days.

questions.q: Why would a lender name residential tenants as respondents in a foreclosure petition?
choices: To collect the rent arrears from them
To enforce vacant possession against them
To invite them to buy the property first
Because the RTA otherwise forbids foreclosure
questions.explain: Named tenants must leave on the court's possession order, even mid-lease and without RTA notice.

questions.q: What redemption period is typical in an order nisi when the property has equity?
choices: 1 day
6 months
1 year
3 years
questions.explain: Six months. It can be much shorter (even one day) if there's no equity, or the property is abandoned or being wasted.

questions.q: After an order nisi but before conduct of sale, can the owner sell the property?
choices: No, only the lender can sell
Yes, during the redemption period
Only with the court's permission first
Only to the lender
questions.explain: The owner can list and sell during the redemption period without court supervision.

questions.q: What happens to the owner's listing when the lender gets an order for conduct of sale?
choices: It continues until it expires on its own
It ends; the lender takes over marketing
It becomes an exclusive listing for the lender
It automatically converts to a public auction
questions.explain: The owner's right to list and market ends, and any existing listing is terminated.

questions.q: At the hearing to approve a foreclosure sale, how can another buyer compete?
choices: By phoning the judge
With one sealed, higher offer
By matching the accepted price
By making a backup offer
questions.explain: Interested parties get one chance to submit a sealed offer that must be higher; the court usually approves the highest.

questions.q: On a court-approved sale, which is usually paid first?
choices: The lender that petitioned the court
Outstanding property taxes and utilities
The listing brokerage's real estate commission
The second mortgage, ahead of the first
questions.explain: Taxes and utilities, then priority strata fees, commission, the petitioning lender plus costs, then the balance into court.

questions.q: What does a lender give up by taking an order absolute?
choices: Any right to possession of the property
The right to sue on the personal covenant
The right to sell the property later on
Its first-ranking priority over other charges
questions.explain: Under PLA s.32, after order absolute the lender can't pursue the borrower or guarantor for any shortfall.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Order absolute vs judicial sale

questions.q: After a judicial sale for less than the debt, is the borrower liable for the shortfall?
choices: No, the debt is extinguished
Yes, the borrower remains liable
Only if they are a corporation
Only the guarantor is liable
questions.explain: After a judicial sale, borrowers (and guarantors) remain liable for any deficiency. After order absolute, they aren't.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Order absolute vs judicial sale

questions.q: How does an agreement for sale differ from a vendor take-back mortgage?
choices: The buyer pays no interest on the balance
The seller stays the registered owner
The buyer can't take possession until paid
It can't be registered at the land title office
questions.explain: Under an agreement for sale the seller remains on title until paid; the buyer's interest is a registered charge (Form C).

questions.q: What is the cash-equivalent price of an offer with vendor financing?
choices: Cash down plus the mortgage face value
Cash down plus the mortgage's market value
The stated offer price, always
The mortgage's face value alone
questions.explain: Cash down plus the present value of the mortgage payments discounted at the market rate.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · How financing changes what an offer is worth

questions.q: A VTB's contract rate is below the market rate. How does the offer's real value compare with its stated price?
choices: It is higher than the stated price
It is lower than the stated price
It is exactly equal
It can't be determined
questions.explain: The see-saw: a below-market rate makes the mortgage worth less than face, so the offer is worth less.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · How financing changes what an offer is worth

questions.q: A seller offers a below-market VTB. How can they reduce the value they give away, keeping the same rate?
choices: Lengthen the amortization period
Shorten the mortgage term
Lower the down payment
Remove the due on sale clause
questions.explain: A shorter term limits how long the below-market rate lasts, raising the mortgage's market value.

questions.q: When calculating a VTB's market value, which rate do you use to find the PV in step 2?
choices: The contract rate
The current market rate
The prime rate
The stress test rate
questions.explain: Payments come from the contract rate; the market value comes from discounting them at the market rate.

questions.q: When valuing an assumed mortgage, what do you enter as N?
choices: The original amortization in months
The number of payments remaining
The number of payments already made
Always 300
questions.explain: Only the payments the buyer will make (remaining in the term, or remaining amortization if fully amortized).

questions.q: How should an appraiser treat a sale that included below-market assumed financing?
choices: Use the sale price unchanged
Adjust out the financing benefit
Add the financing benefit to the price
Average it with the list price
questions.explain: The recorded price includes a financial asset. The appraiser must isolate and remove it, or exclude the comparable.

questions.q: What's the main catch with porting a mortgage to a new home?
choices: Ports are banned in BC
You must re-qualify, within a time limit
The rate resets to posted rates
The lender charges 3 months' interest
questions.explain: You usually need to re-qualify under current rules (stress test) and complete within a window (often 30–120 days).

questions.q: How does a fee deducted from the advance affect the borrower's true cost?
choices: It lowers the true cost
It raises the true cost
It has no effect
It only affects the lender
questions.explain: The borrower pays interest on the full face value while receiving less cash, so the real rate is higher than the contract rate.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Bonuses, brokerage fees and the true cost of borrowing

questions.q: What must BC lenders disclose to consumer borrowers under the BPCPA?
choices: The cost of funds advanced
The annual percentage rate (APR)
The lender's own cost of funds
The broker's commission split
questions.explain: The APR: the contract rate plus non-interest finance charges. COFA isn't legally required.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Bonuses, brokerage fees and the true cost of borrowing

questions.q: When calculating cost of funds advanced on a partially amortized loan, what goes into PV?
choices: The face value of the loan
The net amount actually received
The outstanding balance at term end
The total of all payments
questions.explain: Payments come from the gross (face) amount; COFA uses the net cash received as PV, with N = the term.

questions.q: With the same fee, how does a shorter term affect the cost of funds advanced?
choices: It lowers it
It raises it, sometimes sharply
It has no effect
It makes it equal to the contract rate
questions.explain: The fee is recovered over fewer payments, so the effective rate rises. A 5% fee over one year adds roughly 5 points.

questions.q: A lender pays a mortgage broker's fee. What happens to the lender's yield?
choices: It rises above the contract rate
It falls below the contract rate
It equals the contract rate
It becomes zero
questions.explain: The lender pays out more than the loan amount but receives payments based on the loan, so its yield falls.

questions.q: A closed mortgage is paid out early. What penalty do lenders typically charge?
choices: The lesser of 3 months' interest or IRD
The greater of 3 months' interest or IRD
Always 6 months' interest
No penalty under 5 years
questions.explain: Usually the greater of three months' interest or the interest rate differential on the amount prepaid.

questions.q: When is an interest rate differential penalty likely to be large?
choices: When rates have risen since signing
When rates have fallen since signing
When the term just started 1 day ago
Only for variable rate mortgages
questions.explain: The IRD compensates the lender for lost interest when current rates are lower than the contract rate.

questions.q: Which of the five Cs asks whether the borrower CAN repay, using income and debt ratios?
choices: Character
Capacity
Collateral
Capital
questions.explain: Capacity looks at income and debt service ratios. Character asks whether they WILL repay.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · The five Cs of credit

questions.q: A borrower with good credit but self-employment income usually goes to which type of lender?
choices: Prime (A) lender
Alt-A lender
Subprime lender only
No lender will help
questions.explain: Alt-A (A minus) lenders specialize in good-credit borrowers with non-standard income.

questions.q: What is CMHC's minimum credit score for at least one borrower on an insured mortgage?
questions.explain: 680 for at least one borrower. 750+ usually gets the best rates. (600 is the minimum for low-ratio insurance.)
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · The application and credit analysis

questions.q: What minimum down payment does OSFI require for self-employed borrowers at federally regulated lenders?
questions.explain: 35% of the home price.
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · The application and credit analysis

questions.q: How does lending value usually compare with market value?
choices: It is usually higher than market value
It is usually lower, never much higher
It is always exactly equal to market value
It ignores the property's condition entirely
questions.explain: Lending value is long-term and conservative, ignoring speculative factors, so it's usually at or below market value.

questions.q: Lending value is $700,000 and the lender allows 80% LTV. What is the maximum loan on security alone?
What does the gross debt service ratio (as used in this course) include?
choices: All debts, including car loans
Mortgage P + I and property taxes
Only the mortgage interest
Rent and utilities only
questions.explain: GDSR = (principal + interest + taxes) ÷ gross income. TDSR adds all other debt payments.

questions.q: A borrower earns $100,000; the lender's TDSR is 40%; taxes are $4,000 and a car loan costs $6,000 a year. What's the maximum annual mortgage payment?
A borrower qualifies for $520,000 by LTV, $480,000 by GDSR and $455,000 by TDSR. What's the maximum loan?
questions.explain: The lender lends the lowest amount allowed by all constraints.

questions.q: A borrower's contract rate is 2.75%. What qualifying rate applies under the stress test?
Which lender is NOT automatically bound by OSFI's stress test?
choices: A chartered bank
A BC credit union
A federal trust company
A life insurance company
questions.explain: Credit unions are provincially regulated; they apply it only if they choose.

questions.q: How can a borrower qualify for a larger loan without changing their income or the GDSR?
choices: Shorten the amortization period
Lengthen the amortization period
Take a longer fixed term
Increase the property taxes
questions.explain: A longer amortization lowers the payment for a given loan, so the same payment supports more debt (with more risk and interest).
questions.ref: Lesson 13 · Ways to borrow more (and their trade-offs)

questions.q: On a loan at 95% LTV, what is CMHC's premium (traditional down payment)?
questions.explain: 4.00% for 90.01–95% LTV; 4.50% with a non-traditional down payment.

questions.q: What is the minimum down payment for an insured purchase at $800,000?
When the insurance premium is added to the loan, how is it treated in underwriting?
choices: Included in LTV and GDSR
Excluded from LTV; included in GDSR
Included in LTV; excluded from GDSR
Excluded from both ratios
questions.explain: The premium isn't counted in the LTV, but the payments (including it) count in the GDSR.

questions.q: Why should the borrower insure for full insurable value rather than just the loan amount?
choices: Insurers forbid any partial coverage at all
So the lender isn't left sharing the payout
To lower the annual premium the borrower pays
Because CMHC requires it on every single loan
questions.explain: With split policies, the lender may receive only part of a loss payout and be left with damaged security.

questions.q: What does a commercial lender focus on when sizing a loan on an apartment building?
choices: The owner's personal salary
The property's net operating income
The building's assessed value only
The tenants' credit scores
questions.explain: Income property is underwritten mainly on NOI, along with value, borrower track record and tenant strength.

questions.q: NOI is $300,000 and the lender requires a DCR of 1.25. What is the maximum annual debt service?
questions.explain: Maximum debt service = NOI ÷ DCR = $300,000 ÷ 1.25 = $240,000.

questions.q: A lender requires a 20% safety margin on NOI. What is the equivalent debt coverage ratio?
